docs.title: SPARQL for RDF files
docs.text:
sparqld turns a directory of RDF files into a live, read-only SPARQL endpoint. Keep your data in version control and query its current state without importing it into a database.

  • Files stay authoritative

    Use Markdown-LD, YAML-LD, JSON-LD, and the rest of your repository as the source of truth.

  • Queries stay current

    sparqld watches the directory and makes each successful edit available atomically.

  • Safe for people and agents

    The endpoint is permanently read-only: queries explore the knowledge base without changing its files.

docs.title: Serve SPARQL endpoint when its initial dataset is ready
docs.text: Decided · 15 August 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
CI starts sparqld --no-watch over a directory of EARL Turtle reports and then runs several queries against that one dataset. Today, serve_at_with_options loads the complete dataset before it resolves and binds the HTTP addresses, and logs Serving … at … only afterwards. That makes a client infer readiness from a human-readable log line before it can reuse the loaded dataset.

The existing loader builds a fresh store and replaces the shared store only after the complete load finishes (reload_dataset). When watching, the watcher is registered before that initial load so events cannot be missed (DirectoryWatcher::start_with_patterns). The decision must retain those properties while giving CI and long-running clients an endpoint-level startup contract.

flowchart LR CurrentCli["Current CLI start"] --> CurrentLoad["Load complete dataset"] CurrentLoad --> CurrentBind["Bind HTTP listener"] CurrentBind --> CurrentLog["Log Serving"] CurrentLog --> CurrentQueries["Clients query"] DesiredCli["Desired CLI start"] --> DesiredValidate["Validate inputs and addresses"] DesiredValidate --> DesiredBind["Bind HTTP listener"] DesiredBind --> DesiredGate["Root requests wait"] DesiredBind --> DesiredLoad["Load fresh dataset in background"] DesiredLoad --> DesiredPublish["Atomically publish dataset"] DesiredPublish --> DesiredGate DesiredGate --> DesiredQueries["Existing SPARQL dispatch"]

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Startup alternatives compared against the same directory-backed endpoint.

Criterion 2. Bind; wait at ordinary requests 3. Bind; return 503 + readiness route 1. Load before binding 4. Load before binding + ready signal 5. Batch multi-query mode Parse shared dataset once One initial load serves every request. One initial load serves every request. One loaded store serves later requests. One loaded store serves later requests. Could reuse one load within a new batch interface. Correct results while loading Dispatch follows atomic first publication. 503 explicitly declines service while unavailable. No request can arrive before binding. No request can arrive before binding. A process-local batch could query after its load. CI and deployment ergonomics The first normal query is the readiness wait. Requires a client retry or polling policy after 503. Clients need an out-of-band availability check. Requires defining a separate process-signal contract. Does not start the existing HTTP service. Health, readiness, and liveness Readiness is expressed by the normal endpoint, not a probe route. A readiness probe can remove an unready service from traffic. A listening port implies only post-load availability. A signal needs its own health-semantics contract. Provides no long-running endpoint for probes. Timeout, cancellation, and failure Each client keeps its HTTP deadline; shared loading remains independent. 503 communicates temporary unavailability. Connection failures reveal no initialization outcome. Signal consumers need a defined failure and timeout protocol. A separate input protocol must define batch cancellation and errors. Live reload and atomic replacement Retains pre-load watch registration and atomic replacement. Can retain the same watcher and replacement model. Current model already preserves both. Current model already preserves both. A one-shot mode cannot supply live reload. Implementation complexity and API stability Adds one internal readiness gate while retaining /. Adds endpoint and retry contract beyond the existing / API. Preserves the current startup order. Adds a separate readiness-output contract. Adds a second query-supply interface. Outcome Chosen Not selected Excluded—preserves log-coupled startup Excluded—adds out-of-band coordination Excluded—does not improve server startup

Green column: chosen. Yellow column: satisfies the core constraints but was not selected. Red columns: excluded; stronger-red cells identify the decisive shortcoming. denotes a trade-off. The HTTP SPARQL Protocol defines query request forms, while Kubernetes probes distinguish traffic readiness from liveness; sparqld deliberately adds neither /readyz nor /livez, so both continue to be ordinary unknown paths (404) under the root-only handler.

Bind the listener immediately after synchronous validation of the directory, patterns, and resolved addresses. Start the initial load in the background. Until that load reaches a terminal state, every GET or POST request at /, including the landing GET /, waits without a server-imposed deadline. It is then passed to the existing root-only request dispatch.

On success, atomically publish the fresh dataset, release all waiting requests, and run their normal dispatch. Per-file parse errors remain nonfatal: the catalog already records them, so that completed load is ready. A client timeout or disconnect cancels only that request, never the shared load or another waiter. On a fatal initialization failure, pending and subsequent root requests receive 503 Service Unavailable, then sparqld shuts down and exits nonzero without a successful Serving log. Other paths return 404 immediately. After readiness, live reload never re-gates requests and retains staged atomic replacement.

Logs remain informative for people and diagnostics, not a client readiness contract. The existing Serving … at … line remains after readiness for compatibility.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Clients can issue their first ordinary query immediately after starting sparqld, with a client-side timeout appropriate to their CI or deployment.
  • The CLI flags, library function signatures, SPARQL request forms, responses, and non-root 404 behavior remain stable; only the startup timing changes.
  • Release notes document that log parsing is unnecessary and that an immediate root request waits for the initial dataset rather than inferring readiness from the listener or logs.

docs.title: Implementation Steps
docs.text:
• Add an internal, shared initial-load state that wakes all root-request waiters after success or fatal failure.
  • Bind only after validation, begin the initial load in the background, and preserve watcher registration before the first load.
  • Dispatch root requests only after successful first publication; return 503 after fatal initialization and stop the listener before nonzero exit.
  • Document the startup contract in the HTTP API and CLI guidance without introducing a health endpoint.
  • Test listener reachability during load, concurrent GET and POST waiters, atomic complete-dataset results, nonfatal file errors, independent client cancellation, fatal-load 503 and exit, absent probe paths, and post-ready atomic live reload.

docs.text: Decided · 23 August 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text: This ADR evaluates foundations for a generic LSP supporting JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD, without assigning it to a particular consumer.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Parse JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD while preserving authored source spans.
  • Interpret JSON-LD contexts, including @type: @id coercion, to distinguish IRI-valued values from literals.
  • Expose IRI-valued values as clickable document links.
  • Make Go to Definition return every matching definition in the workspace when an IRI has several definitions.
  • Resolve relative local IRIs and support unsaved buffers.

docs.title: Build on JSON-Gold
docs.text:
Excluded alternative universe

This is the excluded alternative universe from the parent ADR.

This planning path uses JSON-Gold as the JSON-LD semantic foundation and builds an LSP around it. JSON-Gold supplies JSON-LD processing, not LSP transport, workspace state, or editor integration; “universe” is planning shorthand for the consequences of committing to this foundation.

piprate/json-gold is a Go JSON-LD processor; its latest v0.8.0 release (2026-02-23) piprate/json-gold is published on GitHub.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Choose a Go LSP framework, transport, document model, position conversion, lifecycle handling, and capability-registration boundaries.
  • Build JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown front-matter syntax layers that preserve source maps from semantic value paths to authored key and scalar ranges.
  • Connect mapped semantic values and JSON-Gold processing piprate/json-gold errors to their original source spans rather than generated JSON text.
  • Define the context, document-loader, and local relative-IRI policy, including contextual base IRIs, permitted local paths, and remote-context handling.
  • Interpret JSON-LD @type: @id coercion to classify IRI-valued scalars, publish clickable links, and return every workspace definition for an IRI.
  • Keep unsaved buffers and incremental edits authoritative for parsing, context loading, diagnostics, document links, and the workspace definition index.
  • Add JSON-LD conformance and LSP end-to-end tests for diagnostic ranges, context errors, @type: @id links, relative cross-file resolution, multiple definition targets, and unsaved edits.
  • Build and distribute a Go binary with editor-installation guidance and file associations for JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD.

docs.title: Universe consequences
docs.text:
• The project owns the LSP transport, incremental document model, syntax parsing, source mapping, navigation, workspace index, and editor-distribution layers around JSON-Gold.
  • The implementation, dependency management, cross-compilation, and release process follow the Go ecosystem.
  • YAML-LD and Markdown-LD require a maintained semantic-value-to-source-span bridge because JSON-Gold processes JSON-LD values rather than authored YAML or Markdown syntax.
  • JSON-Gold dependency and behavioural changes require compatibility tracking behind a stable LSP-facing semantic model.

docs.title: Build on PyLD
docs.text:
Excluded alternative universe

This is the excluded alternative universe from the parent ADR.

This planning path uses PyLD as the JSON-LD semantic foundation and builds an LSP around it. PyLD supplies JSON-LD processing, not an LSP transport, workspace model, or editor integration; “universe” is planning shorthand for the consequences of committing to this foundation.

digitalbazaar/pyld publishes the Python PyLD package for JSON-LD processing.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Choose the Python LSP runtime, transport, document model, position conversion, lifecycle handling, and capability-registration boundaries.
  • Build JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown front-matter syntax layers that preserve a source map from semantic value paths to authored key and scalar ranges.
  • Adapt mapped semantic values for PyLD processing digitalbazaar/pyld while retaining path associations for diagnostics and semantic results.
  • Translate PyLD processing failures into diagnostics at original JSON, YAML-LD, or Markdown-LD source spans rather than generated JSON text.
  • Define the context, document-loader, and local-IRI resolver policy, including contextual base IRIs, relative document resolution, permitted local paths, and remote-context handling.
  • Interpret JSON-LD @type: @id coercion to classify IRI-valued scalars, publish clickable links, and return every workspace definition for an IRI.
  • Keep unsaved buffers and incremental edits authoritative for parsing, context loading, diagnostics, document links, and the workspace definition index.
  • Maintain a workspace index of definitions and references that updates as in-memory and on-disk documents change.
  • Add PyLD, LSP-protocol, and end-to-end tests for diagnostic ranges, context errors, @type: @id links, relative cross-file resolution, multiple definition targets, and unsaved edits.
  • Publish a Python package and editor integrations, including file associations for JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD.

docs.title: Universe consequences
docs.text:
• The project owns the LSP transport, incremental document model, syntax parsing, source mapping, navigation, workspace indexing, and editor-distribution layers around PyLD.
  • The implementation and release toolchain follow the Python ecosystem, including its LSP-client and editor-extension packaging conventions.
  • YAML-LD and Markdown-LD need a maintained semantic-value-to-source-span bridge because PyLD processes JSON-LD values rather than authored YAML or Markdown syntax.
  • PyLD dependency and behavioural updates need compatibility tracking behind a stable LSP-facing semantic model.

docs.title: Build on Qlue-ls
docs.text:
Excluded alternative universe

This is the excluded alternative universe from the parent ADR.

This planning shorthand assumes that Qlue-ls IoannisNezis/Qlue-ls supplies the LSP foundation. The resulting server replaces or generalizes its SPARQL-specific language intelligence for JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD.

Qlue-ls is a Rust SPARQL language-server library with native and WASM server entry points; its documented distribution also supports an installed command and editor clients.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Map Qlue-ls’s server lifecycle, document store, URI handling, position conversion, capability registration, and diagnostics interfaces; isolate components that can remain language-neutral.
  • Replace or generalize the SPARQL parser, formatter, completion, and query-execution pipeline so JSON-LD documents become first-class inputs without retaining SPARQL assumptions.
  • Build a YAML-LD syntax tree and source map that map semantic values and JSON-LD paths to YAML key and value spans.
  • Extract Markdown-LD front matter, retain its document offset, and translate JSON-LD diagnostics and navigation ranges back into the Markdown buffer.
  • Select and integrate a JSON-LD processor, including context loading, relative-IRI resolution, local-document policy, and error translation to source ranges.
  • Interpret @type: @id coercion to classify IRI-valued values; publish document links and Go to Definition results for every matching workspace definition.
  • Make in-memory, unsaved buffers override on-disk documents for parsing, context resolution, indexing, and navigation.
  • Establish JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD conformance fixtures plus end-to-end LSP tests for diagnostics, links, single and multiple definitions, relative IRIs, and unsaved edits.
  • Package the resulting server, document editor configuration and file associations, and verify native and WASM/editor integration paths.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Decide whether Qlue-ls’s SPARQL capabilities remain in the same distributable or are separated before semantic-web features and configuration are generalized.
  • Audit every reused protocol and workspace component for coupling to SPARQL AST types, endpoint-driven completion, and query-specific configuration.
  • Carry the maintenance cost of a downstream fork or coordinate upstream abstractions before relying on Qlue-ls as the common LSP base.
  • Verify that the required YAML-LD and Markdown-LD processing, filesystem access, and local-document policies work consistently in both Qlue-ls native and WASM targets.

docs.title: Build on rdflangserver
docs.text:
Excluded alternative universe

This is the excluded alternative universe from the parent ADR.

This path is unavailable as a PyPI dependency today, but it records what would change if rdflangserver became publishable. It would use rdflangserver as the Python LSP foundation and generalize its RDF language support for JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD.

niklasl/rdflangserver declares repository version 0.1.0-dev pyproject.toml; the corresponding rdflangserver PyPI package is unavailable.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Publish and release a stable rdflangserver package with a versioned compatibility policy before making it a dependency.
  • Audit the PyGLS and RDFLib boundaries for LSP lifecycle, document storage, URI handling, position conversion, diagnostics, and workspace synchronization.
  • Add JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD syntax layers that retain mappings from semantic-value paths to authored key and scalar spans.
  • Connect a JSON-LD processor to the mapped semantic representation without losing the source locations needed for diagnostics and navigation.
  • Define context loading and local-IRI policy, including relative resolution, permitted local files, document bases, and remote-context handling.
  • Recognize @type: @id coercion, expose IRI-valued scalars as clickable links, and return every matching workspace definition.
  • Make unsaved buffers authoritative for parsing, context resolution, diagnostics, document links, and the definition index.
  • Maintain an incremental workspace index of IRI definitions and references across JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD.
  • Add processor, source-map, and end-to-end LSP tests for source ranges, context failures, IRI links, relative cross-file navigation, multiple definitions, and unsaved edits.
  • Publish the generic server and document editor integrations and file associations for JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD.

docs.title: Universe consequences
docs.text:
• Adoption cannot begin until a supported package is released; the project must either sponsor that release or carry a forked distribution.
  • The implementation, dependency management, and editor integration follow the Python and PyGLS ecosystems.
  • YAML-LD and Markdown-LD require a maintained semantic-value-to-source-span bridge because JSON-LD processors do not preserve their authored syntax locations.
  • The project must track upstream changes in rdflangserver, PyGLS, RDFLib, and the selected JSON-LD processor behind a stable LSP-facing model.

docs.title: Build on SHACLC Language Server
docs.text:
Excluded alternative universe

This is the excluded alternative universe from the parent ADR.

This planning shorthand assumes that SHACLC Language Server jeswr/shaclc-language-server supplies the LSP foundation. This universe extracts or generalizes its VS Code-oriented boundary, then replaces its SHACL Compact Syntax pipeline with support for JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD.

SHACLC Language Server is available as a published VS Code Marketplace extension, providing an installable starting point for assessing its server and extension boundaries.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Evaluate reusable VS Code extension and LSP boundaries, and determine whether a generic server can be extracted without retaining editor-specific assumptions.
  • Replace the SHACL Compact Syntax parsing and analysis pipeline with JSON-LD processing while preserving protocol-facing language features.
  • Build a YAML-LD syntax tree and source map from semantic values and JSON-LD paths to YAML key and value spans.
  • Extract Markdown-LD front matter, retain its document offset, and translate JSON-LD diagnostics and navigation ranges back into the Markdown buffer.
  • Integrate a JSON-LD processor with explicit context loading, local-IRI policy, relative-IRI resolution, and diagnostic-to-source-range translation.
  • Interpret @type: @id coercion to classify IRI-valued values; publish document links and Go to Definition results for every matching workspace definition.
  • Make in-memory, unsaved buffers override on-disk documents for parsing, context resolution, indexing, and navigation.
  • Add protocol and end-to-end tests for diagnostics, links, relative IRIs, single and multiple definitions, and unsaved edits through a non-VS Code client.
  • Package a generic server and editor integrations, then document independent installation and file associations beyond the Marketplace extension.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Separate reusable LSP code from the SHACLC VS Code extension and its SHACL Compact Syntax assumptions.
  • Maintain the replacement JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD semantic pipeline as a downstream architecture.
  • Maintain compatibility tests across the Marketplace extension and at least one non-VS Code client.
  • Establish and maintain a generic-server distribution channel in addition to the extension package.

docs.title: Build on Sophia JSON-LD
docs.text:
Excluded alternative universe

This is the excluded alternative universe from the parent ADR.

This planning path uses Sophia JSON-LD as the semantic foundation for a new language server, rather than as an LSP implementation. “Universe” is planning shorthand for the consequences of committing to this foundation.

Sophia JSON-LD pchampin/sophia_rs is the sophia_jsonld parser-and-serializer package in Sophia pchampin/sophia_rs; its manifest Cargo.toml depends on json-ld 0.15.1 and offers optional file: and HTTP and HTTPS context retrieval.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Create the Rust LSP transport, lifecycle, document model, workspace store, and request routing that Sophia does not provide.
  • Parse JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD into one document model while retaining a source map from JSON-LD value paths to JSON, YAML, or embedded-front-matter spans.
  • Design and implement a mapped-input adapter from each document model to Sophia JSON-LD parsing and serialization APIs pchampin/sophia_rs, retaining enough semantic provenance to return LSP ranges.
  • Configure a context and document-loader policy around Sophia’s optional file and HTTP context features Cargo.toml, including local-document access, permitted remote access, and relative-IRI base resolution.
  • Interpret JSON-LD type coercion to @id so IRI-valued strings are distinguished from literals and surfaced as clickable LSP document links.
  • Build an IRI definition index and serve every matching workspace target through the LSP definition response.
  • Make semantic conversion, source maps, document links, and the definition index update from authoritative unsaved text on open and full-document change notifications.
  • Translate parser, context, and semantic errors back through the source map to exact JSON, YAML, or Markdown diagnostic ranges.
  • Add JSON-LD conformance fixtures and LSP end-to-end tests for diagnostics, @type: @id links, relative cross-file resolution, Markdown offsets, unsaved buffers, and multiple definition targets.
  • Package the Rust binary and provide editor integration, installation, versioning, and release automation.

docs.title: Universe consequences
docs.text:
• Own the full LSP implementation and its editor-facing compatibility surface.
  • Maintain adapters and source maps across three authored syntaxes while following Sophia and its json-ld dependency releases.
  • Establish and maintain the server’s context-loading, workspace-indexing, and navigation policies as product behaviour.

docs.title: Build on Stardog Language Servers
docs.text:
Excluded alternative universe

This is the excluded alternative universe from the parent ADR.

Planning shorthand for the world in which Stardog Language Servers stardog-union/stardog-language-servers is the LSP base. This page records the work needed to make that base serve generic YAML-LD and Markdown-LD, not a decision to do so.

The upstream project is a TypeScript Lerna and Yarn-workspaces monorepo stardog-union/stardog-language-servers whose documented servers support multiple LSP transports and diagnostics, hovers, and completion stardog-union/stardog-language-servers.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Map the repository's transport, document lifecycle, workspace, and request-dispatch APIs; separate reusable LSP infrastructure from Stardog-language stardog-union/stardog-language-servers-specific semantics.
  • Establish a TypeScript runtime, build, test, and published-package path for a generic standalone language server, independent of Stardog Studio and its extensions.
  • Add a YAML-LD parser that retains source ranges and maps YAML nodes to JSON-LD values without round-tripping through generated JSON text.
  • Add Markdown-LD extraction for frontmatter, translating YAML ranges back to Markdown-document offsets.
  • Integrate a JSON-LD processor with an explicit context-loading policy and a local-IRI resolver shared by JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD documents.
  • Interpret @type: @id coercion to classify values as IRIs or literals; expose IRI values as document links and return every matching workspace definition.
  • Make incremental analysis use unsaved document buffers rather than only files on disk.
  • Create fixtures and end-to-end LSP tests for diagnostics, source ranges, local and relative IRIs, multiple definitions, document links, and unsaved edits.
  • Package, version, and release the generic server; verify editor integration through the documented stdio installation path stardog-union/stardog-language-servers.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Maintain a TypeScript toolchain and release process alongside any Rust-based linked-data consumers.
  • Audit and either isolate or replace Stardog-specific parsing and semantic dependencies before publishing a generic server.
  • Own source-map correctness across YAML frontmatter and full Markdown files, including edits that move frontmatter offsets.
  • Define and test the security and caching behavior of JSON-LD context loading and local IRI resolution.

docs.title: Build on SWLS
docs.text:
Chosen alternative universe

This is the chosen alternative universe from the parent ADR.

This planning path uses SWLS as the LSP foundation and extends it for YAML-LD and Markdown-LD. “Universe” is planning shorthand for the consequences of committing to this foundation.

SemanticWebLanguageServer/swls is a Rust LSP that already supports JSON-LD alongside Turtle, TriG, and SPARQL.

docs.title: JSON-LD parser
docs.text: SWLS directly uses rdf-parsers 0.1.16: its JSON-LD language implementation mod.rs calls parse_incremental to retain a lossless concrete syntax tree, then convert_with_loader to obtain the semantic model and active context. OxJSONLD oxigraph/oxigraph appears elsewhere among SWLS’s resolved dependencies, but is not its direct JSON-LD parser.

docs.title: First release
docs.text:
YAML-LD only

The first release supports YAML-LD. Markdown-LD extraction and range translation are follow-up work.

docs.title: SWLS execution path
docs.text:
backend.rs handles didOpen by creating a document entity with Source, RopeC, Label, Open, and other generic components. The resulting CreateEvent lets a registered language attach its marker; the parse schedule then runs. On didChange, SWLS replaces only Source and RopeC before running that same schedule again. The JSON-LD language system parses changed open documents, converts the syntax tree into an Element and active context, then reruns the shared derivation schedule mod.rs. Go to Definition injects the cursor position into a separate request schedule, which searches every document’s derived triples and maps matching subject spans back through RopeC goto_definition.rs.

flowchart LR OpenChange["didOpen or didChange"] --> DocumentEntity["Source, RopeC, Label, Open"] DocumentEntity --> LanguageMarker["YAML-LD language marker"] LanguageMarker --> ParseSchedule["ParseLabel"] ParseSchedule --> YamlAdapter["YAML adapter and source map"] YamlAdapter --> SemanticElement["Element and active context"] SemanticElement --> Derivations["triples, diagnostics, links, definitions"]

docs.title: Establish the extension boundary
docs.text:
• Record the reusable generic components—Source, RopeC, Label, Open, Dirty, and Element—and the JSON-LD-specific marker and active-context components document.rs.
  • Define a YamlLdLang marker, a YAML-LD source-map component, and a parse system whose output is the shared Element model plus JSON-LD active context.
  • Register the YAML-LD language identifier and file association using the existing language-registration path lib.rs.
  • Prove that opening and fully replacing a minimal YAML-LD document creates and updates the YAML-LD entity without changing existing JSON-LD behaviour.

docs.title: Map YAML-LD source
docs.text:
• Parse YAML while retaining key and scalar spans.
  • Convert the YAML structure to the JSON-LD-shaped input required by the semantic layer, recording a mapping from each resulting JSON-LD value path to its YAML source span.
  • Route YAML syntax, conversion, and JSON-LD semantic diagnostics through that map, so the editor never reports a position in generated JSON text.

docs.title: Derive link semantics
docs.text:
• Pass the mapped YAML-LD structure through SWLS’s existing JSON-LD conversion, which already applies type coercion to @id; record which converted values are IRIs and retain their YAML source ranges rather than reimplementing coercion.
  • Add a textDocument/documentLink result path for those mapped IRI ranges, resolving each target against the document base. Do not reuse SWLS’s DocumentLinks component: it represents imported documents, not clickable value ranges.

docs.title: Index workspace definitions
docs.text:
• Build or extend the workspace index so each IRI definition retains its document URI and mapped source range.
  • Extend SWLS’s go-to-definition request path backend.rs to return every workspace definition matching an IRI-valued link.
  • Recompute the derived graph, source map, links, and definition index from authoritative in-memory text on open and full-document change notifications, before a disk scan can overwrite unsaved state.

docs.title: Release evidence
docs.text:
• Add end-to-end fixtures through SWLS’s LSP feature test harness SemanticWebLanguageServer/swls for YAML-LD diagnostic ranges, @type: @id links, relative cross-file resolution, multiple definitions, and unsaved edits.
  • Package the extended server and verify its editor distribution path with SWLS’s documented binary and editor integration model SemanticWebLanguageServer/swls.

docs.title: After first release
docs.text: • Define a context-loader policy that replaces or constrains SWLS’s context loader mod.rs, which can request HTTP contexts, then implement the selected local-context security rules and IRI resolution policy.

docs.title: Markdown-LD
docs.text:
• Identify YAML front matter and report malformed or missing delimiters against Markdown-document ranges.
  • Feed extracted front matter through the YAML-LD mapper while translating every resulting range by the front-matter offset.
  • Keep the containing Markdown document authoritative for open and unsaved-buffer updates.

docs.title: Universe consequences
docs.text:
• Upstream changes to SWLS core and language crates SemanticWebLanguageServer/swls become an ongoing compatibility and release-management concern.
  • A YAML-LD source-map layer and Markdown front-matter adapter would be new language implementations alongside SWLS’s existing JSON-LD language crate SemanticWebLanguageServer/swls, so their parsing, semantic mapping, and tests require local maintenance.
  • Replacing the current context-loading behaviour mod.rs risks duplicating or diverging from upstream JSON-LD conversion and navigation logic.

docs.title: Build on Turtle Language Server
docs.text:
Excluded alternative universe

This is the excluded alternative universe from the parent ADR.

This planning path builds the server on Turtle Language Server. “Universe” is planning shorthand for the consequences of committing to this foundation.

BrickSchema/langserver is a Python language server for Turtle, published as turtle-language-server.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Evaluate the reusable pygls lifecycle and document synchronization server.py, separating protocol plumbing from Turtle-specific behaviour.
  • Generalize Turtle and RDFLib-backed language behaviour BrickSchema/langserver into JSON-LD-aware analysis without regressing Turtle documents.
  • Implement a YAML AST adapter that retains authored key and scalar spans while producing JSON-LD values.
  • Extract Markdown front matter and map every embedded YAML range back through its containing Markdown offset.
  • Select a JSON-LD 1.1 processor and context model and implement a safe relative-IRI resolver shared by all three document formats.
  • Interpret @type: @id coercion to classify IRI values, expose clickable document links, and return every target through Go to Definition.
  • Make the derived graph, ranges, links, and definition index follow the authoritative in-memory open and change notifications before workspace files on disk.
  • Add pytest-based fixtures BrickSchema/langserver and end-to-end LSP tests for diagnostic ranges, Markdown offsets, relative IRIs, multiple definitions, links, and unsaved edits.
  • Publish a Python package and validate editor deployment through the turtle-language-server installation channel.

docs.title: Universe consequences
docs.text:
• Maintain a Python and pygls runtime, including its LSP lifecycle and editor-distribution compatibility.
  • Own a new JSON-LD semantic layer and its context-loading, IRI-resolution, and source-map policies beside the original Turtle/RDFLib implementation.
  • Maintain YAML-LD and Markdown-LD parsers, mappings, and incremental-edit tests that the Turtle server does not provide.
  • Separate generic server packaging and documentation from the Brick-specific identity of the existing published package.

docs.title: Build on vscode-jsonld
docs.text:
Excluded alternative universe

This is the excluded alternative universe from the parent ADR.

This planning path assumes that vscode-jsonld becomes an installable LSP foundation. It is currently unavailable through the VS Code Marketplace; this page records the work that would become necessary if publication made that foundation usable.

alexkreidler/vscode-jsonld declares repository version 1.0.0 package.json, but its expected VS Code Marketplace item is absent.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Publish a release and an installable extension or standalone server package before depending on this code as an LSP foundation.
  • Audit the VS Code extension and language-server boundary; extract a generic server interface that does not require the VS Code extension host.
  • Implement YAML-LD parsing with a source map from JSON-LD value paths to authored YAML key and scalar spans.
  • Extract Markdown-LD front matter, preserve its document offsets, and map diagnostics and navigation ranges back to the Markdown buffer.
  • Define JSON-LD context loading, local-document access, and relative-IRI base-resolution policies before connecting semantic processing to workspace files.
  • Interpret @type: @id coercion to distinguish IRI-valued strings from literals; emit clickable document links and all matching workspace definitions.
  • Make in-memory, unsaved buffers authoritative for parsing, context resolution, indexing, links, and navigation.
  • Test the extracted generic server with at least one non-VS Code LSP client, including diagnostics, links, multiple definitions, relative IRIs, and unsaved edits.
  • Distribute the generic server independently, document editor configuration and file associations, and keep the extension package aligned with it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Maintain a fork or upstream a generic server boundary if the extension’s architecture cannot be reused without VS Code assumptions.
  • Own the YAML-LD and Markdown-LD parsers, source mappings, workspace index, and their regression suites.
  • Operate and support a publication channel that does not exist for this project today.
  • Track compatibility between the generic server, the VS Code extension, and other LSP clients as separate release surfaces.

docs.title: Render ASK answers as SPARQL boolean values
docs.text:
The MkDocs pluglet parses an ASK response as a Python boolean. Direct template rendering must produce the SPARQL spellings true and false so authors can show query answers consistently.

Verify both answers in rendered MkDocs pages. Keep query and data fixtures in the shared example sources.

docs.title: Declare reproducible project settings
docs.text:
Define a project configuration contract that contributors can check into version control. Document how command-line arguments override project settings so a shared project produces predictable behavior across machines.

This outcome is a prerequisite for the remote-data goal, which needs an explicit policy for approved hosts.

docs.title: Reproduce the MkDocs SPARQL demo
docs.text:
Make the MkDocs integration example reproducible from its documented data and query sources. A contributor should be able to build the example and compare the rendered answer with the documented result.

Use the same scenario files for documentation and integration tests. See the MkDocs integration for the current pluglet setup.

docs.title: Discover the query service
docs.text:
Expose a service description that standards-aware clients can obtain from the endpoint. This lets clients identify the query service from its address and connect using their discovery behavior.

Verify discovery with a client that uses service descriptions. The client documentation gives Comunica an explicit endpoint source type.

docs.title: Count shared triples once
docs.text:
A triple present in several source graphs must count once when a query reads the union default graph. Preserve the regression test identified in this record when updating Oxigraph.

The recorded prerequisite is an Oxigraph release containing the upstream fix for repeated triples. Track the defect in the GitHub issue and the fix in the upstream pull request.

docs.title: Load embedded graph IRIs with fragments
docs.text:
Investigate the recorded loading failure for embedded graph IRIs containing fragment identifiers. Preserve the full graph IRI when loading the embedded RDF data.

Establish a regression scenario with a fragment-bearing graph IRI. Verify that the graph loads and its statements remain queryable.

docs.title: Query a watched directory from Obsidian
docs.text:
Provide an Obsidian plugin workflow for querying RDF in a watched directory. Users should be able to run SPARQL from their vault and inspect the answer while sparqld tracks file changes.

Verify the workflow with a vault example, including a query after a source file changes.

docs.title: Install the pluglet on Python 3.11 and 3.12
docs.text:
The Python package currently requires Python 3.13 or later. Broaden pluglet compatibility so MkDocs projects on Python 3.11 and 3.12 can install it.

Verify package installation and a documentation build on each supported version. Check dependency constraints as part of that compatibility work.

docs.title: Opt in to inferred statements
docs.text:
Choose inference semantics before implementing this outcome. The inference decision compares the available approaches and blocks this goal.

The resulting workflow must let users enable inferred statements while keeping their asserted source data unchanged. Verify query answers and source data preservation with a shared example scenario.

docs.title: Query cached remote Linked Data
docs.text:
Combine local data with cached Linked Data obtained from explicitly approved remote hosts. Establish the approval policy through the project configuration goal before adding remote access.

Verify local and cached remote facts in one query. Check that remote requests follow the configured host policy.

docs.title: Retrieve large query results progressively
docs.text:
Deliver query results progressively so large answers do not require buffering the complete response before transmission. This goal concerns response delivery for users retrieving large result sets.

Verify that a client receives result data before query output is complete. Measure response buffering with a result set large enough to expose full response allocation.

docs.title: `j lint` failing
docs.text: …and is not run in CI

docs.title: Run MkDocs queries through the native Python API
docs.text: Use the native sparqld Python API for MkDocs macro queries. Install it as a dependency of mkdocs-macros-sparqld so ordinary builds do not need a separate server or binary.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• Query the shared Rust engine through the Python package, reusing a loaded dataset per directory during a build.
  • Preserve existing macro behavior, result rendering, diagnostics, and query semantics. Define and test refresh behavior for mkdocs serve and cleanup across builds.
  • Preserve a way to run HTTP endpoint examples, including the existing sparqld_port and endpoint helper contracts or a documented migration for their users.
  • Test a clean installation, a strict MkDocs build, multiple directories, query failures, and live reload. Inspect rendered documentation in Chromium through Playwright.
  • Update installation and integration documentation and run the required MkDocs review.

Prerequisite: https://github.com/iolanta-tech/sparqld/issues/41.

docs.title: Add integration coverage for HTTP and MCP query semantics
docs.text:
Add integration coverage that loads anonymized source files and queries the real engine through both HTTP and stdio MCP. This is deferred work.

Acceptance: - Verify SELECT, ASK, CONSTRUCT and DESCRIBE results, malformed-query errors, and update rejection through both interfaces. - Verify that a triple repeated across source files contributes once to the default union, while explicit GRAPH matches preserve source graph identity. - Preserve legitimate duplicate solution bindings from joins, equal projected values and multivalued metadata. - Cover OPTIONAL plus correlated NOT EXISTS: missing and mixed statuses, multiple companies, self/other awaiting-response holds, blockers and submitted applications. Keep fixtures synthetic. - Use semantic assertions and deterministic checks in CI; keep timing/scaling experiments in a separate bounded benchmark. - When query-timeout is implemented, add HTTP/MCP parity checks for SELECT/ASK/graph timeouts, discarded partial results, a subsequent successful query, independent concurrent deadlines, and dataset access being released after cancellation.

Existing tests/mcp.rs provides a starting point. Exercise the loader and public interfaces rather than replacing the query engine with mocks. The default-union correctness assertion should expose the currently known upstream defect until that dependency fix is adopted.

docs.title: Default union double-counts triples shared by source files
docs.text:
The default union counts an identical triple once per source graph. This inflates aggregates and multiplies join results in both HTTP and MCP queries.

Reproduce with two files:

first.ttl: 

<urn:example:subject> <urn:example:value> 10 .

second.ttl: 

<urn:example:subject> <urn:example:value> 10 .

Serve their directory and run: 

SELECT (COUNT(*) AS ?count) (SUM(?value) AS ?total)
WHERE { ?subject <urn:example:value> ?value }

Expected: count = 1, total = 10. Actual: count = 2, total = 20.

Control: 

SELECT (COUNT(*) AS ?count)
WHERE { GRAPH ?graph { ?subject <urn:example:value> ?value } }
The control should still return count = 2 because the source graphs are distinct.

Verified on 20 October 2026 using the union-default-graph API used by sparqld: - Locked Oxigraph 0.5.9 / spareval 0.2.6: duplicate count = 2. - Latest released Oxigraph 0.5.12 / spareval 0.2.8: duplicate count = 2. - Oxigraph 0.6.0-dev at 7ce152a1d910d5662027a5bcbe7c32cee0a4e059: correct count = 1.

Upstream issue: https://github.com/oxigraph/oxigraph/issues/1919 Merged fix: https://github.com/oxigraph/oxigraph/pull/1920 Latest release checked: https://github.com/oxigraph/oxigraph/releases/tag/0.5.12

The fix is on the development branch and is absent from 0.5.12. An ordinary update within the current 0.5 requirement does not resolve it. The development revision was verified in an isolated engine harness; compatibility with the complete sparqld application has not been tested.

Acceptance: - Adopt a released dependency containing the fix, or a separately reviewed and validated backport/development pin. - Return correct COUNT/SUM over shared triples through HTTP and MCP. - Preserve explicit GRAPH identity and legitimate duplicate solution bindings from distinct matches. SELECT DISTINCT is not a substitute for correcting the union. - Retain a synthetic regression fixture and record the tested dependency versions.

Integration coverage: https://github.com/iolanta-tech/sparqld/issues/25

docs.title: Add a shared query timeout for HTTP and MCP
docs.text:
Long-running queries currently have no server-side execution deadline. Stopping an async wait does not stop the blocking query computation.

Add the same optional CLI setting to both interfaces:

sparqld /path/to/data --query-timeout 20
sparqld mcp /path/to/data --query-timeout 20

Use one shared execution policy rather than separate timeout implementations in the HTTP and MCP adapters. Leaving the option unset preserves unlimited execution.

Acceptance: - Parse a positive whole number of seconds and reject zero, invalid and overflowing values. - Give each query an absolute deadline and an Oxigraph cancellation token. Cover planning, evaluation, full result iteration and server-side response preparation; define startup, input-reading and network-write boundaries consistently. - Signal engine cancellation when the budget expires. Discard buffered partial results and check the absolute deadline immediately before publishing success, including ASK and MCP output packing. - Return an explicit timeout error through both interfaces. Proposed encoding: HTTP 503 with a query-timeout message; MCP tool result with isError=true and the same reason. Keep client cancellation distinct from deadline expiry. - Bridge MCP request cancellation and handler cleanup to engine cancellation. Do not rely on dropping or timing out spawn_blocking. - Remove completed deadline registrations and retain worker/resource accounting until execution actually stops and releases dataset access. - Test HTTP/MCP parity, SELECT/ASK/graph cancellation, late timer delivery, independent concurrent deadlines, a successful query after a timeout, and reload progress after cancellation.

Oxigraph 0.5.9 already exposes SparqlEvaluator::with_cancellation_token, so engine cancellation does not require a dependency upgrade. A temporary probe stopped evaluation at a 100 ms deadline. However, cancelled ASK/EXISTS probes on 0.5.9 and 0.5.12 returned a successful boolean with the token already cancelled. A final deadline/cancellation check is therefore necessary even if evaluation returns success.

Document that cancellation is cooperative: sorting and other work between engine checkpoints may overshoot. A strict process-termination boundary would require isolated query workers and is separate architectural work.

Integration test tracking: https://github.com/iolanta-tech/sparqld/issues/25

docs.title: Remove the dataset RwLock
docs.text:
The dataset is shared as Arc<RwLock<Store>> (SharedDataset), but the lock protects nothing that Oxigraph does not already guarantee.

Why it is unnecessary:

  • oxigraph::store::Store is Clone (a handle to shared storage) and thread-safe. Its in-memory backend gives each query a consistent snapshot while writes proceed.
  • Watch-mode reloads already mutate the store in place under a read guard (watcher::reload), relying on that guarantee rather than on the lock.
  • The only write-lock acquisition is reload_dataset in src/lib.rs, which swaps in a freshly loaded store. It runs only during initial load (both --no-watch and watch mode via DirectoryWatcher::start_with_patterns), before StartupGate is marked ready.
  • HTTP and MCP queries wait on StartupGate before taking the read lock, so once a query reaches the lock no writer can exist. Acquisition never blocks; it only adds poisoning error paths and a lock-wait boundary that has to be reasoned about.

Proposal:

Have the initial load publish its finished Store through the startup gate (for example a OnceLock<Store>, or a gate that carries the store on Ready), and give queries and the watcher a Store clone instead of a lock guard.

Acceptance:

  • Remove RwLock from SharedDataset and all read()/write() call sites in server.rs, mcp.rs, watcher.rs and lib.rs, together with their lock-poisoning error handling.
  • Preserve startup behaviour: queries wait until the initial load finishes and receive the existing error if it fails.
  • Existing HTTP, MCP and watcher tests pass; reload visibility tests still observe in-place updates.

This also removes the lock-wait boundary from the query-timeout design in https://github.com/iolanta-tech/sparqld/issues/27.

docs.title: Resolve remote JSON-LD contexts from project RDF
Why
docs.text:
Project data can reference remote JSON-LD contexts, but sparqld currently supports only bundled and project-local contexts. Let an explicit project pipeline supply downloaded bodies, then describe their locations in RDF.

Prerequisite: structured missing-context errors in the RDF file catalog. That is separate, planned work.

docs.title: What
docs.text:
Recognize ordinary project RDF declaring a context URI as jsonld:Context with a schema:contentUrl pointing to its local body:

"@context":
  - https://json-ld.org/contexts/dollar-convenience.jsonld
  - jsonld: http://www.w3.org/ns/json-ld#
    contentUrl:
      "@id": https://schema.org/contentUrl
      "@type": "@id"

$id: https://example.org/context
$type: jsonld:Context
contentUrl: ./example-body.jsonld
  • Query the existing RDF graph directly when the JSON-LD loader requests a context. Do not introduce a separate URI-to-file index.
  • Allow declarations anywhere among included project sources. Give .contexts/ no special meaning.
  • Support arbitrary absolute context URIs, including HTTP, IPFS, IPNS, DID, and NI identifiers.
  • Use contentUrl as the sole new body mechanism. Support JSON bodies in .json and .jsonld, and YAML-LD bodies in .yamlld.
  • Resolve relative file references using the declaration document’s existing base rules. Keep referenced files inside the served project, including through symlinks.
  • Preserve the requested context URI as the loaded body’s logical document URL. Resolve nested context references against that URI, then use the same RDF lookup.
  • Preserve existing bundled dollar-context and direct local-context support.

docs.title: Loading and reloads
docs.text:
1. Parse currently resolvable sources into RDF.
  2. Use the structured RDF errors to identify sources blocked by missing context registrations.
  3. Retry them as new declarations become available.
  4. Stop when all sources finish or a round makes no progress. Keep unresolved dependencies visible in the error catalog.

Let the existing JSON-LD processor handle context arrays, scoped contexts, @import, and recursion limits.

Preserve incremental reloads. Track dependencies on body files and all sources contributing registration triples. Resolve against staged contributions plus unaffected published RDF, excluding replaced sources’ old graphs. Propagate changes and deletions transitively.

Identical declarations may coexist. Different targets for one context URI must fail startup or reject a reload batch before publication. Preserve existing per-source handling for ordinary parsing failures.

docs.title: Acceptance
docs.text:
• Load a source that sorts before its declaration, including declaration chains.
  • Resolve nested contexts using their remote logical base rather than the local body directory.
  • Cover arbitrary URI schemes, JSON/YAML bodies, and bodies excluded from ordinary RDF ingestion.
  • Report missing registrations, bootstrap cycles, malformed bodies, ambiguous targets, and path escapes.
  • Recover after adding or repairing a declaration or body.
  • Reload consumers after declaration/body edits or deletions; preserve unrelated sources.
  • Test declaration triples split across source graphs and identical declarations in several sources.
  • Keep existing bundled and local context tests passing.
  • Document runnable YAML-LD examples from dedicated files and verify their rendered documentation through Playwright.

Downloading and updating artifacts remain explicit pipeline operations, for example through Make, DVC, or Vitrify.

docs.title: Use `sparqld` from Python
docs.text: Provide import sparqld through a thin native Python binding to the shared Rust dataset and query API. Python applications should load a project and run SPARQL without starting an HTTP server.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• Expose a documented dataset lifecycle and query API. Define Python result types and surface load and query errors as Python exceptions.
  • Reuse the Rust library's loading, catalog, source graph, default graph, and query behavior.
  • Support repeated queries against the same dataset and define reload or watch behavior.
  • Build and distribute installable wheels for supported Python versions and platforms. Verify a clean installation without a separately installed sparqld executable.
  • Test SELECT, ASK, and graph queries against real fixture directories, errors, and parity with existing interfaces.
  • Document a runnable Python example and review the MkDocs documentation.

Prerequisite: https://github.com/iolanta-tech/sparqld/issues/62.

docs.title: Stream graph update events
docs.text:
• File deleted
  • File added
  • File changed
  • ...

Applications should be able to subscribe on such atomic events. This enables, say, live update interfaces; might be also useful for agents.

docs.title: Add Vault-LD to the living file-backed SPARQL alternatives ADR
docs.text:
The living alternatives ADR says to revisit its comparison when new alternatives appear. Vault-LD is not listed.

Vault-LD defines a Markdown-vault format whose frontmatter is interpreted as YAML-LD through shared contexts. It adds Vault-LD-specific processing, including [[wiki links]] resolved to IRIs, plus tools to export and ingest RDF: - Vault-LD specification - Vault-LD repository and tools

Please update the ADR to evaluate Vault-LD against its existing criteria. The comparison should make the unit clear: Vault-LD provides a vault format and RDF import/export tools, while the ADR compares live queryable graph services. Its documented tools do not appear to provide a live watcher or SPARQL endpoint, so consider whether to compare Vault-LD alone or as part of a stack with a query service.

Also state which semantics the YAML-LD and Markdown-LD columns mean. In particular, distinguish sparqld's Markdown-LD definition (YAML-LD frontmatter) from Vault-LD's extension syntax and processing rules.

Acceptance criteria: - Add Vault-LD or a clearly justified equivalent solution to the ADR comparison. - Evaluate it using the same capability criteria and cite current primary sources. - Record any limits or assumptions, including whether an external SPARQL service is needed. - Clarify the local meanings of YAML-LD and Markdown-LD in the comparison.

docs.title: Expose a reusable Rust dataset and query API
docs.text: Expose the dataset and query engine as a reusable Rust library, so applications can load and query a project without starting a server.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• Provide a documented public API to open a directory-backed dataset and execute SPARQL queries, with useful errors returned to the caller.
  • Share the existing source loading, catalog, query semantics, and query policy with the HTTP and MCP interfaces.
  • Support repeated queries against a loaded dataset. Define ownership, cleanup, and whether callers can request reloads or watching.
  • Do not terminate the host process on library errors.
  • Test SELECT, ASK, and graph queries, load errors, query errors, and parity with the existing interfaces.
  • Document a runnable Rust example and review the MkDocs documentation.

This API is a prerequisite for the Python integration in https://github.com/iolanta-tech/sparqld/issues/41.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Get a first successful query against a directory of RDF files.

  • Starting with Agents

    Install the skill and ask your coding agent to set up the knowledge base.

  • Starting in CLI

    Install sparqld and sq, serve a directory, and run a SPARQL query.

docs.title: Starting with Agents
docs.text:
Install the sparqld skill for your coding agent:

npx skills add iolanta-tech/sparqld --skill sparqld -g

Ask the agent to set up the knowledge base:

/sparqld set up a queryable knowledge base at my documents folder

Approve installing sparqld and registering the MCP server when it asks. Then ask it about the knowledge base; it should answer from SPARQL and show the queries it ran.

With example Alpha Centauri data configured, this session used its query tool to find the recorded planets:

Youuser.prompt

In $sparqld, find information about known planets in Alpha Centauri system, and show me the query you used to obtain that.

Codexcodex.response

Using the sparqld skill, I inspected the knowledge base vocabulary and followed the recorded star and system links. It records two planets in the Alpha Centauri system: Proxima Centauri b and Proxima Centauri d.

The query and its result are shown below.

See Agents for each coding agent and the MCP contract. Prefer Starting in CLI when you want to drive SPARQL yourself.

docs.title: Starting in CLI
docs.text:
This guide needs Cargo. Install Rust and Cargo if it is not already available.

Install sparqld with Cargo:

Command

cargo install sparqld

Install ktk/sq to send the query:

Command

cargo install --git https://github.com/ktk/sq

cargo install sq installs the wrong package

The crates.io crate named sq is unrelated. Use the GitHub install above.

docs.title: Serve a directory
docs.text:
Create a directory for the data:

Command

mkdir -p data

In your editor, create data/alpha-centauri.md and paste this source:

Source alpha-centauri.md

---
"@context":
  schema: https://schema.org/
  dbo: http://dbpedia.org/ontology/
  dbp: http://dbpedia.org/property/
  dbr: http://dbpedia.org/resource/
  $: schema:name
  constellation:
    "@id": dbo:constellation
    "@type": "@id"
  contains:
    "@id": schema:hasPart
    "@type": "@id"
  is-orbited-by:
    "@reverse": dbp:star
$id: dbr:Alpha_Centauri
$: Alpha Centauri
schema:description: The closest star system to the Solar System.
constellation:
  $id: dbr:Centaurus
  $: Centaurus
contains:
  - $: Alpha Centauri AB
    contains:
      - $type: dbo:Star
        $: Alpha Centauri A
      - $type: dbo:Star
        $: Alpha Centauri B
    is-orbited-by:
      - $id: dbr:Proxima_Centauri
        $type: dbo:Star
        $: Proxima Centauri
        is-orbited-by:
          - $id: dbr:Proxima_Centauri_b
            $type: dbo:Planet
            $: Proxima Centauri b
          - $id: dbr:Proxima_Centauri_d
            $type: dbo:Planet
            $: Proxima Centauri d
---

# Alpha Centauri

Alpha Centauri is the closest star system to the Solar System.

Start sparqld in this terminal:

Command

sparqld ./data

Keep this terminal running. The endpoint is available at http://127.0.0.1:7737/ and watches the directory for changes.

docs.title: Query the endpoint
docs.text:
Open a second terminal. This query shows what orbits what in the example.

Save it as orbits.rq:

Source orbits.rq

PREFIX schema: <https://schema.org/>
PREFIX dbp: <http://dbpedia.org/property/>

SELECT ?body ?orbits
WHERE {
  ?bodyResource dbp:star ?parent .
  ?bodyResource schema:name ?body .
  ?parent schema:name ?orbits .
}
ORDER BY ?body

Run it with sq:

Command

sq -e http://127.0.0.1:7737/ -f orbits.rq

Result orbits.tsv

Proxima Centauri    Alpha Centauri AB
Proxima Centauri b  Proxima Centauri
Proxima Centauri d  Proxima Centauri

Each row is a body followed by what it orbits.

Queries are read-only, so exploring the dataset cannot modify your files.

docs.title: See a live update
docs.text:
In data/alpha-centauri.md, change Alpha Centauri to a new name and save the file. Run the same sq command again: the result changes without restarting sparqld.

Browse the compatible SPARQL clients for other ways to query the endpoint, or prefer Starting with Agents for the skill-based path.

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text:
sparqld [OPTIONS] <DIRECTORY>

  • <DIRECTORY>

    Required · Directory to serve

  • --host <HOST>

    Listening address · Default 127.0.0.1

  • --port <PORT>

    Listening port · Default 7737

  • --no-watch

    Load once without watching for file changes

  • --pattern <GLOB>

    Include or exclude source paths; repeat for multiple patterns

  • --query-timeout <SECONDS>

    Stop queries that run longer than this many seconds · Default unlimited

  • -h, --help

    Show command help

  • -V, --version

    Show the installed version

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
sparqld mcp [--pattern <GLOB>]... [--query-timeout <SECONDS>] <DIRECTORY>

mcp exposes the directory to an MCP client over standard input and output and always watches it for source changes.

  • <DIRECTORY> is required.
  • Repeat --pattern <GLOB> to include or exclude source paths, using the same pattern rules as the HTTP server.
  • --query-timeout <SECONDS> works the same as for the HTTP server.
  • --host, --port, and --no-watch apply only to the HTTP server; mcp does not accept them.

docs.title: Combine options
docs.text:
Options can be composed in any order:

Command

sparqld ./examples --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --no-watch

docs.title: Limit query time
docs.text:
--query-timeout takes a positive whole number of seconds. Leaving it unset keeps query execution unlimited.

The budget covers parsing, evaluation, reading every result, and building the response. It excludes waiting for the first dataset, reading the request, and sending the response. Each query has its own deadline. Partial results are discarded.

Cancellation is cooperative: sorting, aggregation, and similar work between engine checkpoints can run past the deadline. sparqld does not stop the process.

Command

sparqld ./examples --query-timeout 20

docs.title: Wait for the first dataset
docs.text: The listener binds while sparqld loads its first dataset. Send an ordinary query to / with a client-side timeout; it waits until that dataset is ready. The Serving … at … log line remains useful for people, but is not a client readiness contract.

docs.title: Pattern matching
docs.text:
--pattern matches paths relative to the directory being served. A normal pattern includes matching supported RDF files. Prefix a pattern with ! to exclude matches. When no include patterns are supplied, every supported RDF file remains eligible, so an exclusion alone removes paths from the default set. A plain directory path matches that directory and everything below it.

For example, serve Turtle files while leaving an archive outside the dataset:

Command

sparqld ./data --pattern '**/*.ttl' --pattern '!archive'

Patterns filter source files after sparqld recognizes their extensions. A matching file with an unsupported format remains ignored. Excluded files do not appear in the file catalog. A local JSON-LD context remains available to an included source that declares it, even when the context file is excluded from the dataset.

Warning

--host 0.0.0.0 makes the endpoint reachable from the network. sparqld provides neither authentication nor TLS, so use it only behind controls that restrict access to trusted clients.

docs.title: File catalog
docs.text:
The reserved sparqld: graph describes the served directory. It lets queries relate data to the files and directories from which it came.

Resource RDF types Properties Served directory nfo:FileDataObject, nfo:Folder nfo:fileName Nested directory nfo:FileDataObject, nfo:Folder nfo:fileName, nfo:belongsToContainer Source file with embedded graphs nfo:FileDataObject, sd:Dataset nfo:fileName, nfo:belongsToContainer, sd:namedGraph Named-graph description sd:NamedGraph sd:name Load error rlog:Entry rlog:resource, rlog:level, rlog:message

The source resource IRI is also its named graph IRI. The catalog is updated when source files are created, moved, or deleted.

docs.title: Context dependencies
docs.text:
Each source file links to the context URIs requested while parsing it through jsonld:context. This includes local paths and absolute URIs, including imports and nested context requests. Repeated requests produce one edge. Inline context objects produce no URI edge.

These edges record observed requests, including unsuccessful ones. Each edge starts at the source being parsed; it does not identify which nested context made the request. Parsing can stop before all dependencies are discovered.

After each loading attempt, the catalog replaces that source's dependencies with the requests observed during the attempt. Successful loads retain their dependencies after errors are cleared. Deleting a source removes its outgoing edges. Changes to local context files reload their dependent sources, including sources whose previous loading attempt failed.

This source requests a remote context URL. The catalog records the request whether or not a local body registers that URL:

Source context-dependencies.yamlld

"@context":
  - https://example.org/ctx
  - name: https://schema.org/name

$id: http://dbpedia.org/resource/Alpha_Centauri
name: Alpha Centauri

Unresolved requests also produce dependency edges:

Source missing-context.yamlld

"@context": https://example.org/context
"@id": http://dbpedia.org/resource/Alpha_Centauri
name: Alpha Centauri

Query the catalog to find the context requests:

Source context-dependencies-example.rq

PREFIX jsonld: <http://www.w3.org/ns/json-ld#>

SELECT ?file ?context
WHERE {
  VALUES ?file {
    <sparqld:examples/context-dependencies.yamlld>
    <sparqld:examples/missing-context.yamlld>
  }
  GRAPH <sparqld:> {
    ?file jsonld:context ?context .
  }
}
ORDER BY ?file ?context
file context sparqld:examples/context-dependencies.yamlld https://example.org/ctx sparqld:examples/missing-context.yamlld https://example.org/context

Remote contexts shows an unregistered absolute context URL, registration with vitrify, and the catalog after that body is available.

docs.title: Embedded graphs
docs.text:
For every embedded graph, the catalog uses sd:namedGraph to link the source dataset to an sd:NamedGraph description. Its sd:name is the scoped graph IRI. This is the SPARQL Service Description vocabulary's specific model for named graphs in a dataset.

flowchart TB root["Served directory"] folder["Subdirectory"] source["Source file"] description["Named-graph description"] scoped["Scoped graph IRI"] error["Load error"] folder -->|belongs to container| root source -->|belongs to container| folder source -->|has named graph| description description -->|names| scoped error -->|records resource| source

docs.title: Query the catalog
docs.text:
This query lists every source file and its declared embedded graphs. A source without embedded graphs has an empty ?graph value.

Source file-catalog.rq

PREFIX nfo: <http://www.semanticdesktop.org/ontologies/2007/03/22/nfo#>
PREFIX sd: <http://www.w3.org/ns/sparql-service-description#>

SELECT ?file ?name ?directory ?graph
WHERE {
  GRAPH <sparqld:> {
    ?file a nfo:FileDataObject ;
          nfo:fileName ?name ;
          nfo:belongsToContainer ?directory .
    OPTIONAL {
      ?file sd:namedGraph [ sd:name ?graph ] .
    }
  }
}

docs.title: File formats
docs.text:
sparqld selects a parser from a file's extension. Every source enters its own named graph and shares the same watching and error-reporting behavior. Dataset formats keep their declared named graphs; see Named graphs.

  • JSON-LD

    .json, .jsonld

    Linked data in JSON. Declare terms in the document's @context; the default context already supplies the dollar keyword aliases.

  • YAML-LD

    .yamlld

    JSON-LD authored as YAML 1.2.

  • Markdown-LD

    .md

    YAML-LD front matter. Any YAML front matter is treated as linked data; the Markdown body is ignored, and Markdown without YAML front matter is ignored entirely.

  • Notation3

    .n3

    Compact RDF graph syntax with additional Notation3 features.

  • N-Quads

    .nq

    Line-oriented RDF dataset syntax.

  • N-Triples

    .nt, .txt

    Line-oriented RDF graph syntax.

  • RDF/XML

    .rdf, .xml

    XML serialization of an RDF graph.

  • TriG

    .trig

    Turtle syntax for RDF datasets.

  • Turtle

    .ttl

    Compact RDF graph syntax.

docs.title: Contexts
docs.text: JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD start from the default context and then use the contexts their documents declare. See Contexts.

docs.title: Named graphs
docs.text:
sparqld preserves the boundary between files by loading every source into its own named graph. When a source declares further named graphs, they remain separate and are scoped to that source file.

  • Source graph

    Its IRI is sparqld: followed by the source path relative to the served directory.

  • Default graph

    Queries without GRAPH see the union of every named graph, including the file catalog.

  • Embedded graph

    A graph declared inside a source is named with the source graph IRI, followed by # and its original graph name.

docs.title: Graph IRIs
docs.text:
This documentation site is itself served with sparqld, so paths are relative to the served docs/ directory. For the tangible examples/ directory inside it:

Source path Named graph examples/alpha-centauri.yamlld sparqld:examples/alpha-centauri.yamlld examples/centaurus.md sparqld:examples/centaurus.md examples/proxima-centauri-b.jsonld sparqld:examples/proxima-centauri-b.jsonld

Paths always use / as the separator, and characters that cannot appear literally in the graph IRI are URI-encoded. Renaming or moving a source therefore gives it a new graph IRI.

Use GRAPH to retain source provenance in query results:

Source all-quads.rq

SELECT ?graph ?subject ?predicate ?object
WHERE {
  GRAPH ?graph {
    ?subject ?predicate ?object .
  }
  FILTER(STRSTARTS(STR(?graph), "sparqld:examples/"))
}

docs.title: Named graphs inside a source
docs.text:
TriG, N-Quads, JSON-LD, YAML-LD, and Markdown-LD may declare named graphs. A source's ordinary statements stay in its source graph. Each declared graph is scoped with the source graph IRI, so two files can use the same graph name without colliding.

For example, an assertion graph named http://purl.org/nanopub/temp/np/assertion in nanopublication.yamlld becomes sparqld:nanopublication.yamlld#http://purl.org/nanopub/temp/np/assertion.

References to an embedded graph are rewritten to its scoped IRI too. A nanopublication head therefore continues to point to its assertion, provenance, and publication-info graphs after loading.

flowchart LR source["nanopublication.yamlld"] default["Default-graph statements"] declared["Declared assertion graph"] source_graph["sparqld:nanopublication.yamlld"] assertion["sparqld:nanopublication.yamlld#…/assertion"] head["Head graph links to assertion"] source --> default --> source_graph source --> declared --> assertion head -->|rewritten reference| assertion

The File catalog page describes the reserved sparqld: graph, which records source files, directories, and embedded graphs.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text: Configure your MCP client to launch sparqld mcp <DIRECTORY> over stdio. See the CLI reference for directory and pattern options, or Agents for skill-based setup.

docs.title: Query tool
docs.text:
query accepts one required string argument, query, containing a read-only SPARQL query. The default graph is the union of the loaded source graphs. Queries wait for initial loading; subsequent queries reflect watched file changes.

Every successful tool result contains a JSON object in MCP's structuredContent field. The same object is serialized as JSON in a text block in content for clients that consume text results. The examples below show the value of structuredContent.

docs.title: SELECT
docs.text:
Follows SPARQL Results JSON: head.vars lists the projected variables, and results.bindings contains one object per row. Unbound variables are omitted from that row.

SELECT result mcp-select.json

{
  "head": {"vars": ["value"]},
  "results": {
    "bindings": [
      {"value": {"type": "literal", "value": "first"}}
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: ASK
docs.text:
Uses the SPARQL Results JSON head and boolean members.

ASK result mcp-ask.json

{
  "head": {},
  "boolean": true
}

docs.title: CONSTRUCT and DESCRIBE
docs.text:
Return a sparqld-specific triples array. Each triple has subject, predicate, and object RDF terms encoded as described below. These query forms return a single graph, so triples have no graph-name field. Triple order is unspecified; an empty graph has an empty triples array.

Graph result mcp-graph.json

{
  "triples": [
    {
      "subject": {"type": "uri", "value": "urn:subject"},
      "predicate": {"type": "uri", "value": "urn:predicate"},
      "object": {"type": "literal", "value": "first"}
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: RDF terms
docs.text:
Both bindings and triples use the term representation from SPARQL Results JSON. Each term has a string type and string value:

  • uri: value is the complete IRI.
  • bnode: value is a blank-node identifier without the _: prefix. Its identity is scoped to this result; identifiers cannot be compared across calls.
  • literal: value is the lexical text. Language-tagged literals include xml:lang; other typed literals include the datatype IRI in datatype. Plain string literals omit datatype.

A triple's subject is an IRI or blank node, its predicate is an IRI, and its object can be any of these term kinds.

docs.title: Errors and limits
docs.text:
Tool errors set isError to true and explain the failure in content text.

Condition Result Invalid query or SPARQL Update Error text from evaluation Query larger than 1 MiB in UTF-8 Query is too large Fatal initial dataset failure The load error Query exceeded --query-timeout Same reason text as HTTP Client cancelled the query Server-side work stops at the next checkpoint; no tool result

Change data by editing the source files.

docs.title: Investigation prompt
docs.text: The investigate prompt takes a required question string. It guides the agent to discover the vocabulary, run focused queries, and report evidence with the SPARQL used. Prompt availability in the interface depends on the MCP client.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text: sparqld exposes one read-only SPARQL query endpoint at /.

docs.title: Query requests
docs.text:
The endpoint accepts the SPARQL Protocol GET form and both standard POST forms.

Method Query encoding Content type GET URL-encoded query parameter POST SPARQL query in the request body application/sparql-query POST URL-encoded query parameter in the request body application/x-www-form-urlencoded

A plain GET / returns a text landing response.

docs.title: Startup
docs.text:
sparqld binds its HTTP listener before it finishes the initial directory load. Requests at / wait until that load has published its first dataset, so the first ordinary query can be the readiness wait. Set the HTTP timeout in the client; sparqld does not impose a startup wait deadline. The query timeout starts after this wait, so a client-side timeout is still what bounds readiness.

File-level load errors remain visible in the file catalog and do not prevent the first dataset from becoming ready. A fatal initialization error marks root requests unavailable with 503 Service Unavailable before sparqld exits nonzero; because the process exits immediately, a caller can instead observe a dropped connection.

docs.title: Responses
docs.text:
Query form Content type Body SELECT application/sparql-results+json SPARQL Query Results JSON ASK application/sparql-results+json SPARQL Query Results JSON CONSTRUCT text/turtle Turtle graph DESCRIBE text/turtle Turtle graph

The response serialization is selected by the query form. Accept headers do not currently negotiate another representation.

docs.title: Errors and limits
docs.text:
Status Condition 400 Bad Request Missing, repeated, malformed, or invalid query 404 Not Found Request path other than / 405 Method Not Allowed SPARQL Update or another unsupported HTTP method 413 Payload Too Large Query body exceeds 1 MiB 415 Unsupported Media Type Unsupported POST Content-Type 503 Service Unavailable Fatal initial dataset failure before process exit, or a query that exceeded --query-timeout. The response body tells them apart. 500 Internal Server Error Query evaluation or serialization failure

Error bodies are text/plain. A 405 response includes Allow: GET, POST. Change RDF by editing the served files; SPARQL Update is rejected permanently.

docs.title: Clients
docs.text: This page lists command-line tools that work with sparqld.

docs.title: SPARQL clients
docs.text:
• sq Recommended

    sq -e http://127.0.0.1:7737/ graphs

    Use an endpoint address directly, or configure the endpoint and prefixes for concise repeated queries.

  • Apache Jena rsparql

    rsparql --service http://127.0.0.1:7737/ --query query.rq

  • Comunica

    The sparql@ prefix identifies the source as an endpoint without requiring Service Description discovery.

  • RDFLib sparqlquery

    sparqlquery http://127.0.0.1:7737/ --queryfile query.rq

    Queries the endpoint with RDFLib's Python command-line client.
